summary: This document describes evolving technology in residential networks, with more devices and more internal routing, and defines a general architecture for IPv6 home networking. It sets out principles, considerations and requirements, and highlights implications of using IPv6 at home.

eli5.summary: Homes now have lots of gadgets, not just one computer. This RFC explains how a home network should be organized with IPv6 so everything can find and talk to each other.

questions: why use ula addresses in a home network
subtitle: The principles for a self-configuring IPv6 home network with several subnets and routers.

tldr.problem: Home networks are gaining many devices and internal routing, yet most are single-subnet IPv4 networks hidden behind NAT, and users cannot be expected to configure anything more complex.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets out principles for an IPv6 homenet: reuse existing protocols, support arbitrary topologies and multihoming, delegate prefixes automatically, use ULAs for stable internal addressing, route internally, apply border filtering, and provide naming and service discovery across subnets.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of principles and requirements, not a protocol, to be observed by later homenet specifications for routing, prefix management, security, naming and service discovery.

Smallest prefix an ISP should offer
facts.value: Not less than a /60; at least a /56 preferred

sections.title: Goals and What IPv6 Changes at Home
sections.content:
The RFC focuses on residential networks with more devices and more internal routing. Today's homes are mostly single-subnet networks provisioned by the ISP as IPv4, often with private RFC 1918 addressing and cascaded NAT. IPv6-capable homes are likely to have several subnets, for example private and guest networks, different link layers and smart grid parts, and enough address space for every device to have a globally unique address. That implies internal routing and an ISP that delegates a large enough block to give each subnet a prefix.

The core assumption is that the homenet is self-organising and self-configuring, without proactive management by the user, though advanced users may override it. The scope is network-layer: addressing, connectivity, routing, naming and service discovery, not user interfaces or link layers. IPv4 is not changed, and the network may be IPv6-only or dual stack. The CE router requirements in RFC 7084 are treated as out of scope.

The RFC lists several effects of IPv6. Multiple subnets and routers raise the question of how to allocate prefixes and extend single-subnet service discovery. Global addressability removes the need for NAT but turns the question into one of reachability. Devices become multi-addressed, with a link-local address, one or more global addresses, possibly a ULA, and privacy addresses. Users should not be expected to type IPv6 literals, so naming and discovery are imperative.
sections.eli5: In the old days a house had one network and one door to the Internet. Now it has many rooms with different kinds of wires, so the network has to decide for itself how to give each room an address, without asking you.

sections.title: Topologies, Multihoming and Self-Organisation
sections.content:
The architecture should not assume a topology, because people plug devices together in ingenious ways. Loops in a routed topology are good because they offer redundancy, and a failure should leave as much of the network working as possible. The RFC describes three example models: one ISP with one CE router and internal routers, two ISPs with two CE routers on a shared subnet, and two ISPs with one CE router on a shared subnet. For dual stack, the general recommendation is to follow the same topology for IPv6 as for IPv4 but without NAT.

Multihoming is expected to become more common. Hosts should be multi-addressed with a global address from each ISP's delegated prefix, and must pick source and destination pairs, commonly by RFC 6724. A packet must leave through the ISP whose prefix matches its source address or upstream ingress filtering (BCP 38) may drop it. Options mentioned include source-based routing, passing per-prefix information to hosts, or routing on source as well as destination address. NPTv6 is not recommended.

The network should also be able to subdivide itself into the largest practical subnets, cope with links of very different speeds (the RFC cites 1 Mbit/s up to 1 Gbit/s), and detect realms and borders, such as the ISP, the homenet and a guest network, at which sharing of prefixes, routes, discovery and names can be limited. The default inside the homenet is to share everything. An owner should be able to claim their devices securely, for example by pressing buttons on an authenticated and a new device, so that neighbouring homenets stay separate.
sections.eli5: People will plug boxes together in odd ways, so the network must still work. It also needs to know where your home ends and the street begins, like a fence around the garden with a gate.

sections.title: Addressing, Prefixes and ULAs
sections.content:
A homenet may receive an arbitrary-length prefix such as /60, /56 or /48 from its ISP, and should assume nothing about its stability or length. The RFC assumes ISPs follow BCP 157 (RFC 6177), under which end sites can always obtain a reasonable amount of address space. A CE router should ask via DHCP Prefix Delegation for a /48, the largest it might expect, even if it is offered only a /56 or /60. It is not recommended for an ISP to offer less than a /60 and highly preferable that it offers at least a /56. If the prefix is too small, the router should enter an error state and warn, rather than use subnets longer than /64, NPTv6 or bridging.

Unique Local Addresses (RFC 4193) should be used alongside global prefixes, on all devices, to give stable communication between subnets when the ISP prefix changes or external connectivity is down, and to let constrained devices keep permanent relationships. ULAs do not imply NAT or NPTv6. A device with both addresses should use the ULA internally and the global address externally, and the border routers should filter ULA source and destination addresses. A single /48 ULA across the homenet is desirable, though the network must still work with more than one.

Internal prefix assignment should be autonomous, efficient, avoid duplicate /64s, and give each link a stable prefix that survives reboots and does not depend on router boot order. If the ISP forces a sudden renumbering, the homenet must cope with a flag-day style event, not the graceful process of RFC 4192. The RFC makes no specific recommendation for the delegation method, but all routers in a homenet very likely need to use the same one.
sections.eli5: The ISP lends the house a big block of street numbers, and the house hands out smaller ranges to each room. Rooms also get private house-only numbers that never change, even if the street numbers do.

sections.title: Routing Inside the Homenet
sections.content:
Routing is needed once there are several routers. It could be as simple as the IPv4 NAT model of a default route being up, but more likely involves a routing protocol. A mechanism is required to discover which router provides the CE function, and the routing environment must be self-configuring and interact predictably with homenet self-configuration at startup and reconvergence.

The protocol should be based on a previously deployed protocol shown to be reliable and robust, and suitable for lightweight implementations in consumer devices. At most one unicast and one multicast routing protocol should be in use at a time, and if routers support several, they must all agree on one. The architecture is agnostic on link state versus Bellman-Ford. It should support multiple Internet connections and delegated prefixes, ideally deciding on source and destination addresses to avoid ingress filtering problems, and routing within the homenet should continue without ISP connectivity.

Because of diverse links, path selection may be better than hop count, and traffic may use multiple paths. Convergence should not be much longer than the outage users already accept when their CE router reboots. Low-power and lossy networks (LLNs) are treated as stub areas that do not carry transit traffic. Multicast routing, including source-specific multicast, is desirable across the homenet, with scoping so that it is not flooded onto media that cannot support it. Routing between the CE router and the service provider is out of scope.
sections.eli5: When a house has several routers, they need to share a map so a message can find its way from room to room. The map should draw itself and keep working even when the Internet is down.

sections.title: Security: Addressable Is Not Reachable
sections.content:
Removing NAT brings global addressability, so the RFC distinguishes addressability from reachability: a device can have a global address yet be unreachable because of a firewall. RFC 4864 describes a stateful 'Simple Security' model, and RFC 6092 expands it without mandating 'default deny', requiring an easily selected transparent mode. The IETF discussed 'default deny' against 'default allow' at length without consensus, so the RFC makes no recommendation beyond RFC 6092, but says CE routers should keep the option of 'default deny'. A 'default deny' approach replaces NAT traversal with a signalling protocol such as PCP to open a firewall hole.

The RFC admits that both NAT and firewalls are only partially effective, since a compromise of one device behind them exposes all the others, but notes that poor default device security makes a firewall useful. Border filtering should be easy for users to adjust, for example giving a guest access to a printer. It also flags exfiltration, where devices use discovery to gather information and report it to vendors, and says hosts should apply their own security in line with their capabilities. With proper filtering on the CE router, a ULA source address can serve as a hint that traffic is local. The formal Security Considerations section just refers to this discussion.
sections.eli5: Every house can now have its own street address, but that does not mean strangers should be let in. A gate at the border decides who may come to the door, and the owner can open it for friends.

sections.title: Naming and Service Discovery
sections.content:
Devices need unique names and a way to find each other, such as media servers and printers, with as little management as possible. Naming and discovery should span the whole homenet, ignoring subnet borders but respecting policy borders such as the guest network. Existing zero-configuration discovery protocols are generally aimed at single subnets, so the choice for multi-subnet homes is to proxy or extend them, for example by bridging link-local methods without creating loops, widening multicast scope, or a proxy on the CE router. The RFC does not mandate a solution and prefers backward-compatible approaches. It also notes that the number of discovery protocols hurts interoperability.

The homenet name service should support both lookups and discovery, coexist with the Internet name service, and be DNS based or compatible. One suggested set-up is an authoritative server on the CE router plus a secondary from the ISP or a third party. DNSSEC should not be blocked. Remote access needs at least one globally unique name space, by default provided by the ISP, though users may use their own domain. Without one, a local name space is needed, and .local is not suitable because it has link-local meaning for existing protocols. Candidates are an ambiguous space like .sitelocal or a unique one such as .<UniqueString>.sitelocal, where the string might derive from the /48 ULA prefix. Qualified names should always be used.

Name resolution and discovery must keep working when the Internet link is down and survive a full restart, DNS resolver discovery must work several router hops away, and names should ideally follow devices that roam between homenets. Quality of service, operations and management are left neutral: no new QoS protocols are needed, and a separate document is expected for management.
sections.eli5: Nobody wants to remember a long string of numbers for the printer. Devices should pick their own names, announce themselves, and be found by name even when the Internet is off.
